newsitem.title: VIETNAM: U.S. envoy's confirmation lauded by Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy's confirmation lauded by Vietnam.

text.p: Vietnam, almost 22 years to the day after the fall of Saigon, on Friday lauded confirmation of the first U.S. ambassador to Hanoi as a great step in the process of laying to rest the ghosts of war.

Within hours of Douglas "Pete" Peterson's confirmation by the U.S. Senate, officials in the Vietnamese capital gave their first formal comment on an appointment seen by many as long-overdue and mired for months in political controversy.

"I think this is a great step, another big step in the process of normalisation of relations between our two countries," said Peterson's Vietnamese counterpart, Le Van Bang, Hanoi's ambassador-designate to Washington.
"It should be considered as an impetus for better relations in many other fields."

Peterson's confirmation, following a brief Senate debate on Thursday, had been held up for months -- first by a legal technicality and then by charges that Hanoi's efforts to account for Americans missing in action in Vietnam were inadequate.

But news of the decision brought an instant and positive response, uniting the views of Hanoi's small American community with apparatchiks in the government offices of the city centre's Ba Dinh square.

"Through this event we can confirm that now the majority of American people and (the) government in general agree to build up a new kind of relationship with Vietnam." said Nguyen Xuan Phong, director of the Americas department at the foreign affairs ministry. "Of course we are pleased."
U.S. business executives were similarly enthusiastic.

"It's a small victory for us (the U.S. business community)," said Bradley Lalonde of the American Chamber of Commerce. "He embodies Vietnam's attitude towards the struggles of the past and looking towards the future. He'll be well liked."

Peterson's appointment amounts to a psychological landmark in relations between Hanoi and Washington, which a generation after the Vietnam war ended -- in the chaos of April 30, 1975 -- remain fraught with emotion.
The two countries normalised diplomatic ties two years ago, but progress since then towards any kind of normality in the relationship has been painstakingly slow.

While analysts focus on quantifiable measurements, such as the absence of a trade accord, commercial air links and other aspects of a nascent economic relationship, diplomats on both sides concede the real work lies in confidence-building.

An indication of the differences emerged earlier this week when U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, the most senior economic official to visit Vietnam since the end of the war, was castigated, albeit indirectly, by Vietnam's leaders for the slow progress in relations.
For ordinary people, on the streets of this northern capital, reaction on Friday to the news of Peterson's appointment was more down to earth.
"He was a pilot and prisoner of war in Vietnam. It's very good that he's coming back," said a 40-year-old policeman.
"Pete Peterson? Does he work for a bank?" said a young woman.
